text: No new theory in this lesson — four fully worked problems that put the last four lessons to work on fresh numbers, so this arithmetic becomes automatic before eigenvalues and tensor products later in the course.

Problem one: multiply z1 equals 2 plus 3i by z2 equals negative 1 plus 4i. Distributing gives negative 2 plus 8i minus 3i plus 12 i squared; substituting i squared equals negative one turns that last term into negative 12, giving a final answer of negative 14 plus 5i.

Problem two: convert z equals 8 minus 6i to polar form. The modulus is the square root of 64 plus 36, which is the square root of 100, exactly 10. The argument comes out to roughly negative 36.87 degrees — negative because the point sits below the real axis.

Problem three: for z equals negative 2 plus 3i, the conjugate is negative 2 minus 3i. Multiplying them gives 4 plus 9, which is 13. Computing the modulus directly also gives a squared modulus of 13 — both routes agree again, on a number we hadn't used before.

Problem four, two normalization checks: alpha equals the square root of 3 over 2, beta equals i over 2, sums to exactly 1 — a valid state. But alpha equals beta equals 2 thirds sums to 8 ninths, not 1 — not normalized, and dividing both amplitudes by the square root of 8 ninths would fix it.
Chapter 4 picks up from here with the idea every quantum measurement outcome is actually built on: what eigenvalues and eigenvectors mean, starting from scratch.
